title: The 2d Ising Model on Hyperbolic Lattices and the Role of Boundary Conditions
summary: We investigate the role of boundary conditions in the critical behaviour of the ferromagnetic Ising model on regular hyperbolic tessellations. Using worm and Metropolis simulations, we compare open boundaries with wired boundaries implemented through a common auxiliary spin. For open boundaries, the susceptibility exhibits volume-based finite-size scaling with non-mean-field scaling exponents that are approximately stable across four tessellations, supporting the possibility of a common universality class. Comparisons with Binder crossings and susceptibility peaks reveal substantial finite-size effects. For wired boundaries, the central-to-auxiliary spin correlator exhibits radial scaling consistent with a mean-field magnetization exponent. The central-spin response to a uniform magnetic field provides a further consistency test of $δ=3$. Layer-resolved responses to a weak boundary field also reveal an enhancement of the induced magnetization towards the interior. Our results highlight the importance of boundary conditions and the distinction between interior and whole-system observables in characterizing critical phenomena on non-amenable lattices.

AI.tldr: The study examines the influence of boundary conditions on the critical behavior of the ferromagnetic Ising model in hyperbolic tessellations, showing that open and wired boundaries lead to different scaling behaviors and highlighting the significance of boundary conditions for characterizing critical phenomena.
AI.motivation: To explore how boundary conditions affect the critical behavior of the Ising model on hyperbolic lattices, which is important for understanding the universality class and finite-size effects in non-Euclidean geometries.
AI.method: The researchers used worm and Metropolis algorithms to simulate the Ising model with both open and wired boundary conditions. They analyzed the susceptibility, Binder crossings, and spin correlators, as well as the response to magnetic fields at the boundary and center of the lattice.
AI.result: For open boundaries, the system showed volume-based finite-size scaling with non-mean-field exponents, while for wired boundaries, a mean-field magnetization exponent was observed. The study also found significant finite-size effects and an enhancement of induced magnetization towards the interior of the lattice when applying a weak boundary field.
AI.conclusion: The research underscores the impact of boundary conditions on the critical properties of the Ising model on hyperbolic tessellations, and it suggests that observables from the interior of the lattice may be more indicative of the true critical behavior than whole-system measurements.

title: Exact and Near-Exact Inverse Renormalization Group with Constrained Monte Carlo
summary: We establish conditions for exactness of the inverse renormalization group via constrained Markov processes, a class of Monte Carlo simulations which sample the degrees of freedom within a block on a fine lattice under the constraint that they remain consistent with the corresponding degree of freedom on the coarse lattice according to a forward renormalization group transformation. We show analytically, for an arbitrary transformation, that constrained Markov processes correspond to an exact inversion of the renormalization group at the fixed point action, and to a near-exact inversion in the vicinity of the fixed point. We then optimize renormalization group transformations directly on inversely renormalized configurations to effectively map the action onto itself and ensure computational stability in the generation of configurations for high-dimensional systems. Starting from a set of uncorrelated configurations for the three-dimensional $φ^{4}$ quantum field theory at lattice volume $V=16^{3}$, we invert the renormalization group with constrained Monte Carlo to construct a set of uncorrelated, near-equilibrium configurations for $V=128^{3}$ and extract two critical exponents of the system. The inversion exhibits no critical slowing down, with dynamic critical exponent $z=0.03(2)$.

AI.tldr: The paper explores the conditions for exactness of the inverse renormalization group using constrained Markov processes, showing that they correspond to an exact inversion at the fixed point action and a near-exact inversion nearby. It optimizes transformations on inversely renormalized configurations, ensuring computational stability. Using this method, it generates uncorrelated, near-equilibrium configurations for high-dimensional systems and extracts critical exponents, with no critical slowing down observed.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to establish a reliable and stable method for inverting the renormalization group, which is essential for studying the behavior of physical systems across different scales, especially in high-dimensional spaces. The aim is to avoid critical slowing down and achieve accurate results for critical exponents of systems such as the three-dimensional φ⁴ quantum field theory.
AI.method: The method involves using constrained Markov processes, a form of Monte Carlo simulation, to sample degrees of freedom within blocks on a fine lattice while maintaining consistency with degrees of freedom on a coarse lattice. The authors also optimize renormalization group transformations directly on the inversely renormalized configurations, allowing for the effective mapping of the action onto itself and ensuring computational stability.
AI.result: The result is the successful generation of uncorrelated, near-equilibrium configurations for a 3D φ⁴ quantum field theory at a larger lattice volume (V=128³) from a smaller one (V=16³). The researchers were able to extract two critical exponents of the system, demonstrating the absence of critical slowing down with a dynamic critical exponent z=0.03(2).
AI.conclusion: The conclusion is that constrained Markov processes can be used to invert the renormalization group exactly at the fixed point and nearly exactly in its vicinity, and this approach can effectively generate configurations for high-dimensional systems without suffering from critical slowing down, providing a robust method for extracting critical exponents.

title: First Overlap Formulation and Perturbative Results for Supersymmetric QCD
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures, Contribution to the 43rd International Symposium on Lattice Field Theory (Lattice 2026)
summary: We present a lattice formulation of N=1 supersymmetric QCD (SQCD) based on overlap fermions, providing a discretization consistent with the Ginsparg-Wilson relation. Particular emphasis is placed on the construction of Yukawa terms that preserve a lattice-modified chiral symmetry involving overlap quarks and gluinos. To realize this modified chiral symmetry in the Yukawa sector, we follow Lüscher's strategy and introduce auxiliary Dirac and Majorana fermionic fields for the quark and gluino fields, respectively. After functional integration over these auxiliary fields, ultralocal interaction terms arise as additional contributions to the lattice action. Within this framework, and using the Wilson gauge action for gluons, we also carry out one-loop perturbative calculations. In particular, we compute the self-energies of the quark, gluon, gluino, and squark fields in the presence of quark and squark masses, enabling an unambiguous determination of the corresponding field and mass counterterms on the lattice. This work provides a robust foundation for future perturbative determinations of the fine-tunings of the gauge, Yukawa, and quartic couplings, and already shows, as expected, a reduction in the number of required counterterms relative to Wilson-type fermions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a lattice formulation for N=1 supersymmetric QCD (SQCD) using overlap fermions, with a focus on constructing Yukawa terms that maintain a modified chiral symmetry. The authors employ auxiliary fields to achieve this and conduct one-loop perturbative calculations, which contribute to the understanding of fine-tuning in SQCD couplings and show a reduced need for counterterms compared to Wilson fermions.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to provide a consistent discretization of N=1 SQCD that preserves chiral symmetry on the lattice, enabling accurate perturbative studies and potentially simplifying the fine-tuning problem associated with different couplings in the theory.
AI.method: The method involves formulating N=1 SQCD on a lattice using overlap fermions, introducing auxiliary Dirac and Majorana fermionic fields to preserve a modified chiral symmetry, and performing one-loop perturbative calculations to determine field and mass counterterms.
AI.result: The results include the computation of self-energies for quarks, gluons, gluinos, and squarks, as well as the identification of the necessary counterterms, showing a reduction in the number of required counterterms when compared to formulations using Wilson-type fermions.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion is that the lattice formulation with overlap fermions and the use of auxiliary fields to construct Yukawa interactions provides a solid basis for future perturbative studies in SQCD, particularly for fine-tuning of couplings, and it demonstrates an advantage over Wilson fermions by requiring fewer counterterms.

title: Quark-mass dependence of two-nucleon scattering
summary: Understanding how the properties of the visible Universe depend on the parameters of the Standard Model of particle physics requires \emph{ab initio} theoretical computations. To that end, we investigate the quark-mass dependence of low-energy nucleon-nucleon scattering in the deuteron and dineutron channels. We perform lattice-QCD calculations at pion masses $M_π\approx 200$ and $280$ MeV and compare their results to phenomenology at the physical point and to a previous calculation at $M_π\approx 710$ MeV. Scattering amplitudes, phase shifts, and threshold parameters are determined from finite-volume spectra using quantization conditions that explicitly incorporate long-distance effects from one-pion exchange. We analyze the pion-mass dependence of scattering lengths and effective ranges using chiral effective field theory with Weinberg and Kaplan-Savage-Wise power countings. From this, we estimate the pion-mass derivatives of the inverse scattering lengths and binding momentum, at the physical point. Both power countings indicate that the deuteron unbinds near $M_π\approx 220$ MeV.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the quark-mass dependence of low-energy nucleon-nucleon scattering in the deuteron and dineutron channels using lattice-QCD calculations at different pion masses, and it suggests that the deuteron unbinds near a pion mass of approximately 220 MeV.
AI.motivation: To understand how the properties of the visible Universe depend on the parameters of the Standard Model of particle physics, the authors aim to compute the quark-mass dependence of low-energy nucleon-nucleon interactions ab initio.
AI.method: Lattice-QCD calculations are performed at pion masses of about 200 and 280 MeV. The results are compared with phenomenological data at the physical point and a previous calculation at 710 MeV. Scattering amplitudes, phase shifts, and threshold parameters are derived from finite-volume spectra using quantization conditions that take into account long-distance one-pion exchange effects. Chiral effective field theory with Weinberg and Kaplan-Savage-Wise power countings is used to analyze the pion-mass dependence of these parameters.
AI.result: The analysis provides estimates for the pion-mass derivatives of the inverse scattering lengths and binding momentum at the physical point. Both power-counting methods indicate that the deuteron becomes unbound (unstable) near a pion mass of around 220 MeV.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes with an estimate of the pion-mass derivatives of key scattering parameters and the finding that the deuteron ceases to be a bound state near a pion mass of 220 MeV, which contributes to our understanding of the quark-mass dependence of nuclear forces.

title: Primitive Quantum Gates for an $SU(3)$ Discrete Subgroup: $Σ(216\times3)$
summary: We construct a primitive gate set for the digital quantum simulation of the $648$-element discrete subgroup of $SU(3)$, $\dsb$. The five algorithmic primitives are the inversion, group multiplication, trace, group Fourier transform, and kinetic-phase gates, for which we provide qubit and qutrit--qubit decompositions. For a fiducial shear-viscosity calculation on a $10^3$ spatial lattice with $50$ time steps and a total synthesis-error budget of $10^{-8}$, the estimated fault-tolerant costs are $2.3$--$6.8\times10^{10}$ $T$ gates in the qubit architecture and $1.3$--$5.9\times10^{12}$ $R$ gates in the qutrit--qubit architecture.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a set of basic quantum gates for simulating a 648-element discrete subgroup of SU(3) and estimates the computational cost in terms of quantum gates for a shear-viscosity calculation, comparing qubit and qutrit-qubit architectures.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to develop a gate set that can be used for the digital quantum simulation of a specific subgroup of SU(3), which is important for certain quantum computations, such as those involving particle physics or condensed matter systems.
AI.method: The authors construct a set of five algorithmic primitives (inversion, group multiplication, trace, group Fourier transform, and kinetic-phase gates) with decompositions into qubit and qutrit-qubit operations. They also provide an estimation of the fault-tolerant costs for these operations when applied to a shear-viscosity calculation on a large spatial lattice.
AI.result: For a given shear-viscosity calculation, the estimated fault-tolerant costs are in the range of 2.3-6.8x10^10 T gates for the qubit architecture and 1.3-5.9x10^12 R gates for the qutrit-qubit architecture, assuming a total synthesis-error budget of 10^-8.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes by providing a foundational gate set for the simulation of a discrete subgroup of SU(3) and establishes a basis for assessing the resource requirements for quantum simulations of this type, highlighting the trade-offs between qubit and qutrit-qubit implementations.
